title: Bangers and Mash
subtitle: Sausages, buttery mash, and onion gravy
excerpt: Pork sausages roasted until golden, served on a cloud of buttery mash with a slow-cooked onion gravy. A pub-menu staple that earns its place on the weeknight table.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Sausage and mash as a British working supper, Chapter on Vegetables and side dishes. Nigel Slater, Kitchen Diaries, informal reference for the onion gravy technique and the case for high-welfare sausages.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The onion gravy reheats well. Make it up to two days ahead and keep it in the fridge. The mash is best made fresh.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sauce made from meat juices and stock, thickened with flour and seasoned well. It is the standard accompaniment to roast and grilled meats in British cooking.

content.text: Bangers and mash is the British pub supper at its best: roasted pork sausages on a pile of buttery mash with a thick onion
gravy
. It comes together in under an hour and the oven does most of the work. The sausages go in dry, no oil needed, and roast until the skins split slightly and the fat underneath browns.

A good onion gravy takes time but very little effort. The onions need a slow cook in butter until they are soft and caramel-coloured, then beef stock and a splash of Worcestershire sauce pull it together. Start the onions first, put the sausages in the oven, then cook the potatoes. Everything lands on the table at the same time.
What you need
You need a roasting pan for the sausages, a large saucepan for the potatoes, and a frying pan for the gravy. The sausages need room in the pan, so make sure they fit in a single layer.
Method
Start the onion gravy
Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a wide frying pan over medium-low heat. Add {{onion}} finely sliced onions and stir to coat. Season with a pinch of salt.
Cook, stirring every few minutes, for 25 to 30 minutes until the onions are deep golden and very soft. If they start to stick or colour too quickly, add a splash of water and lower the heat.
Roast the sausages
Heat the oven to 200°C. Put {{sausages-pork}} sausages in the roasting pan in a single layer. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once halfway through, until golden brown all over.
Cook the potatoes and make the mash
Put the quartered {{potato}} of potato in a large saucepan. Cover with cold salted water. Bring to the boil, then cook for 15 to 18 minutes until a knife slides in without resistance.

Drain well. Return the pan to a low heat for one minute to steam off the excess water. Mash thoroughly, then add {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{whole-milk}} of warm milk. Beat until smooth and creamy. Season well.
Finish the gravy

Once the onions are golden, scatter {{plain-flour}} of flour over them and stir for one minute. Pour in {{stock-beef}} of beef stock a little at a time, stirring after each addition to keep it smooth.
Add {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Simmer for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Serve
Pile the mash onto warm plates. Rest two sausages against the mash per person. Pour the onion gravy over the top.

rows.cause: Flour was added too fast or not stirred enough
rows.fix: Push the gravy through a sieve. Next time, add the stock in small amounts and stir constantly while the flour cooks off.

rows.symptom: Sausages split badly and dry out
rows.cause: Oven too hot, or sausages pricked before roasting
rows.fix: Never prick sausages before roasting. Keep the oven at 200°C and turn them once.

rows.cause: Potatoes were overworked or the wrong variety was used
rows.fix: Use a floury potato such as a King Edward or Maris Piper. Mash while hot and stop as soon as it is smooth.

rows.cause: Cooked too fast over too high a heat
rows.fix: Lower the heat and give them more time. Proper caramelisation takes at least 25 minutes.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Bangers and mash has been a British staple since the early twentieth century. The name comes from the sound a cheap sausage makes when it bursts in a hot pan. It sits on every pub menu alongside fish and chips and shepherd's pie. Most people have strong feelings about how it should be made, usually shaped by how their family made it.
